book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: परन्तु ऐसा शासक जिसकी इतिहास में उपस्थिति के सवल प्रमाण हो, जिसके अपने रचे ग्रंथ हो, जिसकी रचना की प्रामाणिकता समकालीन और परवर्ती ग्रन्थकार भी वार-वार प्रकट करते हों, जो विविध झानधाराओं का प्रमाण वन गया हो, जो लोककथाओं तथा अनुश्रुतियों का भी नायक बन गया हो, जिसके मन्दिरों-मूर्तियों-भवनों के निर्माण के प्रमाण सुलभ हों, जिसके ताम्रपत्र और शिलालेख भी प्राप्त हो रहे हों, जिसे तत्कालीन वैदिक औरे जैन सभी समान आदर देते रहे हों - ऐसा अकेला कोई राजा दिखाई देता है, सबसे अधिक जगमगाता कोई शिखर दिखाई देता है तो वह है राजा भोज ।
note: Bhoja as the one ruler with strong historical evidence: own works, temples/images/buildings, copper plates and inscriptions, honoured by Vedic and Jain alike.
gloss: But a ruler whose presence in history rests on strong evidence, who wrote his own works, about whom temple, image and building construction is attested, whose copper plates and inscriptions survive, and whom Vedic and Jain alike honoured - only Raja Bhoja appears as such.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote:
राजा भोज अपने कृतित्व, व्यक्तिव और व्यवहार तथा उदारता के कारण अपने पूरे राज्य में ही नहीं, पूरे भारत में लोकप्रिय रहा । भारत ही नहीं, भारत के वाहर विभिन्न देशों में भी राजा भोज का यश व्यापता रहा । मंगोलिया से वहाँ की मंगोली भाषा में प्राप्त पारंपरिक ग्रन्थ ‘आराजिवुजि’ (राजा भोज) इसका प्रबल प्रमाण है ।
राजा भोज धर्मविद्ध था, वह अपने युग के प्रचलित समस्त धर्मों-सम्पदायों की निजी महत्ता को पहचानता था। इसलिए सबके प्रति उसकी समान आस्था थी।
note: Bhoja's popularity and fame beyond India (Mongolian text), and his equal regard for all sects.
gloss: Raja Bhoja was popular across the kingdom and all India through his works, personality, conduct and generosity; his fame spread abroad, as a Mongolian traditional text on Raja Bhoja shows; he was a knower of dharma who recognised the worth of all prevailing sects and held equal faith in all.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: यही नहीं तुरुक्कों (तुकों) से युध्ध करने पर भी उसने रचनाधर्म में भेदभाव नहीं माना। यही कारण है कि भोज और किसी तुरुक्क (तुकों) कवि की सम्मिलित रचना के प्रमाण कतिपय श्लोक भी पाये जाते हैं।
note: Bhoja fought the Turks yet some verses are joint compositions with a Turk poet.
gloss: Even in fighting the Turks he made no distinction in creative work; verses jointly composed by Bhoja and a Turk poet are found.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote:
राजा भोज ने परम्परानुसार 55 वर्ष 7 मास 3 दिन तक गोड़ देश और दक्षिणापथ सहित विस्तृत क्षेत्र पर राज्य किया था -
पंचाशत्वंचवर्पाणि सप्तमासदिनत्रयम् ।
भोजराजेन भोक्यः सगौड़ो दक्षिणापथः ।।
इससे प्रतीत होता है कि उसने अपने विस्तृत राज्यक्षेत्र पर दीर्घकाल तक शासन किया था ।
note: Tradition of a 55-year 7-month 3-day reign over Gauda and Dakshinapatha.
gloss: By tradition Bhoja ruled 55 years 7 months 3 days over a wide region including Gauda country and Dakshinapatha, which suggests a long rule.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: राजा भोज (999-1055 ई.) इसी सिन्धुराज का पुत्र था। उसके 1010 से 1055 ई. तक के कई ताप्रपत्र, शिलालेख या भूतिलेख प्राप्त होते हैं। एक ताप्रपत्र के अन्त में लिखा गया है - स्वहस्तोयं श्रीभुजदेवस्य । अर्थात् यह (ताप्रपत्र) भोजदेव ने अपने हाथ से लिखा (और दिया) है ।
note: Bhoja (999-1055 CE), son of Sindhurāja; copper plates and inscriptions 1010-1055; a plate signed in his own hand.
gloss: Raja Bhoja (999-1055 CE) was this Sindhuraja's son; several copper plates, stone inscriptions and image inscriptions of 1010 to 1055 CE are found; one copper plate ends 'this is the own hand of Shri Bhojadeva', i.e. Bhojadeva wrote and gave it himself.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: इसी नीति के अधीन चेरीधर, इन्ट रथ, नोगल, भीम के साथ ही कणार्ट, लाट, फुर्नर और तुरुक राजा को भोज ने पराजित किया था। यह उदयपुरा प्रशास्ति ने शिलांकित है।
note: Bhoja's victories over named kings are engraved in the Udaypur praśasti (as the author says).
gloss: Following this policy Bhoja defeated the kings of Chedi, Indraratha, Toggala, Bhima, and also Karnata, Lata, Gurjara and the Turushka king; this is inscribed in the Udayapura prashasti.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: ताम्रपत्रों में भोज के प्रथमों की पुष्पिकाओं में उन्हें 'महाराजाधिराज परमेश्वर श्रीभोजदेव' कहा गया है। स्पष्ट ही राजा भोजीराजाओं के भी राजा थे।
note: Copper-plate colophons style Bhoja 'Maharajadhiraja Parameshvara Shri Bhojadeva'.
gloss: In the colophons of the copper plates Bhoja is called 'Maharajadhiraja Parameshvara Shri Bhojadeva' - clearly a king of kings.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: ऐसे वारह मण्डलों के स्वामी राजा भोज के अधीन थे तव समरांगणसूत्रधार रचा गया। ऐसे मंडलों में अवन्ति मण्डल, पूर्णपथक मण्डल, मोहड़वासक, अर्थाएट मण्डल, स्थाली मण्डल, संगमखेट मण्डल, हूण मण्डल इत्यादि उल्लेखनीय हैं ।
note: Twelve mandalas under Bhoja when the Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra was composed; named mandalas.
gloss: Lords of twelve such mandalas were subordinate to Bhoja when the Samarangana-sutradhara was composed; notable mandalas include Avanti, Purnapathaka, Mohadavasaka, Arthuna, Sthali, Sangamakheta and Huna.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: वैसे विदिशा से भोपाल क्षेत्र में बारहवीं शती में ‘महाढादशकमण्डल’ था। परन्तु वह एक ही मण्डल का नाम था।
note: Mentions Vidisha-Bhopal region's twelfth-century 'Mahadvadashaka-mandala'.
gloss: Moreover, from Vidisha to the Bhopal region there was a 'Mahadvadashakamandala' in the twelfth century, but it was the name of a single mandala.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: भोज परम दानी था । यह कहा जाता था कि श्रुओं को शुंखलावढ़ करने से लोहा और दानपत्र लिखने से भोज के राज्य में ताँव का अभाव होने लग गया था । यह अतिशयोक्ति हो सकती है परन्तु अमूलोक्ति नहीं हो सकती । स्वोक्ति इतिहास से भी यह सिद्ध है कि उसने अपने अनेक श्रुओं को पराजित किया था और अनेक तामप्रन जारी किये थे जिनमें से कुछ तो प्राप्त भी हो गये हैं ।
note: Bhoja's generosity; the claim that copper-plate grants exhausted copper may be hyperbole but not baseless; copper plates issued, some recovered.
gloss: Bhoja was supremely generous; it was said that fettering enemies exhausted iron and writing grant-plates exhausted copper in his kingdom; this may be exaggeration but not baseless, since history shows he defeated many enemies and issued many copper plates, some of which have been found.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: राजा भोज के सुदीर्घ शासनकाल में युद्ध के शंखनाद होते रहे, रणभेरी बजती रही। परन्तु वह शासन के सुनियोजन में दक्ष था। वह योजनावढ़ तरीकेसे शासन करता था। अधिकारीगण अपने-अपने विभाग दक्षता से सम्हालते थे। अतः राजा भोज अपने उन विश्वस्त सहयोगियों के भरोसे निश्चिन्त हो कलासाधना तथा साहित्यसाधना करता रहता था। कवियों, कलाकारों तथा विद्धानों का वह अद्धितीय आश्यदाता था। वह स्वयं गुणी था तथा गुणों का पारखी भी।
note: Bhoja's well-organised administration and unique patronage of poets, artists and scholars.
gloss: Though war-drums sounded through his long reign, he was skilled in administration; officials ran their departments competently, so he could pursue art and literature; he was an unequalled patron of poets, artists and scholars, himself accomplished and a connoisseur.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: भोज न केवल मित्रों अपितु शत्रुओं के लिए भी अपने गुणों में आदर्श रहा । और वे भी भोज के समान स्वयं को घोंपित करवाने में गौरव का अनुभव करते थे । गुजरात के राजा कुमारपाल स्वयं को लघु भोजराज कहलाना पसन्द करते थे ।
note: Bhoja's fame as ideal: Kumārapāla of Gujarat liked to be called 'laghu Bhojarāja'.
gloss: Bhoja was an ideal in virtues for friends and foes alike; they too felt pride in being likened to Bhoja; King Kumarapala of Gujarat liked to be called 'little Bhojaraja'.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: राजा भोज महाराजाधिराज परमेश्वर तो था ही क्योंकि उसके प्रस्थों से भी झात होता है कि उसके अधीनस्थ वारह राजा थे । यह उपाधि उसके ताप्रपत्रों, शिलालेखों तथा प्रस्थों की पुष्पिकाओं में प्राप्त होती है । मालवमण्डन, मालवाधीश, मालवचकवर्ती, सर्वभौम, अविन्तनायक, धारेश्वर, त्रिभुवननारायण, रणरंगमल्ल, लोकनारायण, विदर्भराज, अहिराज या अहीन्द्र, अभिनवाजून, कृष्ण आदि कितने ही विफ्तवों से भोज मण्डित था ।
note: Bhoja's imperial titles and epithets in copper plates, inscriptions and colophons (Mālavacakravartin, Dhāreśvara, Tribhuvananārāyaṇa etc.); twelve subordinate kings.
gloss: Bhoja was Maharajadhiraja Parameshvara, for his works show twelve kings under him; the title appears in his copper plates, inscriptions and colophons; he bore epithets such as Malavamandana, Malavadhisha, Malavachakravartin, Sarvabhauma, Avantinayaka, Dhareshvara, Tribhuvananarayana, Ranarangamalla, Loknarayana, Vidarbharaja, Ahiraja, Abhinavarjuna, Krishna.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: भोज के ज्योतिर्यन्थ राजमूगांक का प्रकाशन ब्रह्मविद्या (4/3) में प्रक्राशित हुआ जो 964 शक (1042 ई.) में रचा गया।
note: Bhoja's astrological work Rājamṛgāṅka composed in Śaka 964 (1042 CE).
gloss: Bhoja's astrological work Rajamriganka, published in Brahmavidya (4/3), was composed in Shaka 964 (1042 CE).
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: यह समस्त वारह राजसमूह जिस राजद्धडामणि की भुजास्तम्भ से वेंधी वृत्ति का है और जिसकी इच्छा से चारों ओर घूमता है। उस श्रीमान् पृथ्वी के एक मात्र राम (तुल्य मनोहर) रा(भो)जदेव ने शीघ्र ही अपनी वृष्टि से यन्त्र प्रपंचों सहित इस यन्त्राध्याय की रचना की 167
note: Colophon verse: the twelve-king circle moves at the will of Bhoja, who composed the yantra chapter (as in the Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra, cf. 31/224).
gloss: This whole circle of twelve kings, whose conduct is bound to the pillar of the arm of that crest-jewel of kings and moves around at his will - that glorious Bhojadeva, the one Rama of the earth, quickly composed this chapter on machines together with these elaborations of devices from his own intellect.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: राजा भोज एक महान् निर्मति था। भोज ने सुरक्षा की दृष्टि से अपनी राजधानी उज्जेन से हटाकर धारा नगरी कर दी। भोज ने उसे नयं ति सरे से वसाया। वह नवनिर्मित नगरी लोकाकर्षक बन गयी थी।
note: Bhoja moved his capital from Ujjain to Dhārā for security and rebuilt it.
gloss: Raja Bhoja was a great builder; for security he moved his capital from Ujjain to Dhara and settled it anew; the newly built city became attractive.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: राजा भोज के समय से मालवा में निर्माण-कांति आ गयी थी। प्रासाद, मन्दिर, तालाव, प्रतिमार्ज़ बनती रहीं और पूरा मालवा इन अनोखी कलाकृतियों से भर गया। मन्दसीर जिला इस दृष्टि से अधिक समुद्ध है। वहाँ का हिंगलाजगढ़ तो तत्कालीन अप्रतिम प्रतिमाओं का अकृत खजाना है। आज मालवा में जो कुछ निर्मितियों के प्राचीन रूप दिखाई देते हैं, उनमें से बहुधा परमारकालीन हैं।
note: Building revolution in Malwa from Bhoja's time; most surviving ancient Malwa structures are Paramāra-period.
gloss: From Bhoja's time Malwa saw a revolution in construction: palaces, temples, tanks and images; Mandsaur district is rich, Hinglajgarh a treasury of images; most ancient structures seen in Malwa today are of the Paramara period.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: यह वताया जाता है कि धारा नगरी में चौरासी चौराहे थे और प्रत्येक पर एक-एक मंदिर था। भोज ने चित्तीड़ में मन्दिर वनवाया था और कश्मीर के कपटेश्वर में कृष्ण सहित मन्दिर वनवाया था।
note: Tradition of 84 crossroads each with a temple in Dhārā; Bhoja's temples at Chittor and Kashmir.
gloss: It is said Dhara had eighty-four crossroads each with a temple; Bhoja built a temple at Chittor and one with Krishna at Kapateshvara in Kashmir.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: भोज ने जो अनेक मन्द्र वनवाये थे उनमें केदार, रामेश्वर, सोमनाथ, मुण्डीर आदि भारत की चारों दिशाओं में थे और मध्य में महाकाल! इसकी पुष्टि उदयपुरा शिलालोख और धार से प्राप्त प्राकृत शिलालोख से भी होती है।
note: Bhoja's temples in the four directions and Mahākāla in the centre; confirmed by the Udayapura inscription and a Dhār Prakrit inscription.
gloss: Among the many temples Bhoja built were Kedara, Rameshvara, Somanatha, Mundira in the four directions of India and Mahakala in the middle; this is confirmed by the Udayapura inscription and a Prakrit inscription from Dhar.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: प्रवन्धचित्नामणि के अनुसार भोज के 104 भवनों, ग्रन्थों और उपाधियों के एक ही नाम थे । इसकी पुष्टि जयवर्मदेव (1258 हैं.) के खण्डित लेख से भी होती है । इसके अनुसार राजा भोज ने 104 मेठ, त्रिकूट आदि प्रासाद वनवाये थे । इससे आगे का लेख खण्डित है । इससे पूर्वांतक प्रवन्धचिन्तामणि की वात की पुष्टि होती है । इन प्रासादों की चर्चा समरंगणसूत्रधार (अध्याय 55-56) में प्राप्त होती हैं ।
note: Prabandhacintāmaṇi's 104 buildings/works/titles of Bhoja, supported by a fragmentary 1258 CE inscription of Jayavarmadeva naming 104 Meru/Trikūṭa-type prāsādas; discussed in Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra chs 55-56.
gloss: According to Prabandhachintamani Bhoja's 104 buildings, works and titles had the same name; this is confirmed by a fragmentary inscription of Jayavarmadeva (1258 CE) saying Raja Bhoja built 104 prasadas such as Meru and Trikuta; the rest is broken; it confirms Prabandhachintamani to that extent; these prasadas are discussed in Samarangana-sutradhara chapters 55-56.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote:
प्रभाच्चाचार्य के अनुसार धारा में 84 प्रासाद और इतने ही चीराहे थे । पूर्वोक्त जयवर्मदेव के 1258 ई. के लेख के अनुसार भोज के मेठ, जिक्रट आदि 104 प्रासाद थे -
नाम्ना यच्यतुरन्तारं शतमियन्मेरुत्रिवादयः ।
प्रसादा: जल……
इससे स्पष्ट है कि 104 की संख्या की पुष्टि साहित्य और शिलालेख दोनों से होती है ।
note: Dhārā had 84 prāsādas/crossroads (Prabhācandra); 1258 CE Jayavarmadeva inscription: 104 prāsādas of Meru, Trikūṭa etc.; number 104 attested by literature and inscription.
gloss: According to Prabhachandra Dhara had 84 palaces and as many crossroads; per Jayavarmadeva's inscription of 1258 CE Bhoja had 104 prasadas such as Meru and Trikuta; so the number 104 is confirmed by both literature and inscription.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: राजा भोज स्वयं महान् निर्माता था । उल्लेखों से स्पष्ट है कि उसने शताधिक प्रासाद तो अपनी राजधानी धारा नगरी में ही वनवाये थे । धारा को उसने व्यवस्थित स्वासा ।
note: Bhoja as builder: references show he built over a hundred prāsādas in Dhārā alone and laid it out systematically.
gloss: Raja Bhoja was himself a great builder; references make clear he built over a hundred palaces in his capital Dhara alone; he planned Dhara in an orderly way.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: मालवा, मेवाङ़ में कितने ही मन्दिर बनवाये, पाठशालाएँ वनवार्थी। भारत की धार्मिक दृष्टि से एकसूत्र में वाँधने के लिए धारी सीमाओं पर केदार, रामेश्वर, सोमनाथ तथा मुण्डीर मन्दिर बनवाये और मध्य के उज्मैन में महाकाल का मन्दिर भी बनवाया। इस प्रक्रिया भोज वास्तुशारत्र और उसके निर्माण की वारीकियों का मर्मजा था। यह न केवल युक्तिकल्पता अविपतु समरांगणसूत्रधार से भी सिद्ध होता है।
note: Bhoja built temples and schools in Malwa and Mewar, temples at the four boundaries and Mahākāla at Ujjain; his architectural expertise shown by Yuktikalpataru and Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra.
gloss: He built many temples and schools in Malwa and Mewar; to bind India together religiously he built Kedara, Rameshvara, Somanatha and Mundira temples on the boundaries and the Mahakala temple at central Ujjain; in this he was a master of vastushastra and its construction subtleties, as both Yuktikalpataru and Samarangana-sutradhara show.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote:
चौसठ पद नामक पूरा नगर कल्पित करें । उसमें सोलह कोष्ठ, छः पथ और नौ चत्वर
(चौराहे) हो 14
चौकोर क्षेत्र में पूर्वे से पश्चिम आते चार भागों में तीन-तीन बॉस (वंश) का विभाजन
करें 15
छः बाँस के इस विभाजन में सोलह पद युक्त होने पर मध्यम वंश पर आश्रित शुभ
राजमार्ग बनाना चाहिए 16
note: The 64-pada town plan with sixteen compartments, six roads and nine crossings; the royal road on the middle bamboo/axis.
gloss: Conceive the whole town as a sixty-four-pada grid, with sixteen kosthas, six paths and nine chatvaras (crossings); divide the square plot into four portions of three vamshas each; in this six-vamsha division of sixteen padas the auspicious royal road should be made on the middle vamsha.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: ज्येष्ठपुर चार हजार चाप (चार कोस या प्रायः बारह किलोमीटर क्षेत्रफल) का होता है। मध्य दो हजार का और एक हजार चाप (एक कोस) व्यास का अधम होता है 12
note: Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra's three grades of town by size (4,000, 2,000, 1,000 cāpa).
gloss: The best town is of four thousand capa (four kos, about twelve km); the middle of two thousand; the lowest is one thousand capa (one kos) in diameter.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote:
जो अशास्त्रज द्वारा और विना लक्षणों के ही किया गया तथा अनुपठान से पवित्र हुए विना ही किया गया वह अप्रशस्त और निष्णल होता है 173
ज्योतिधी और पुरोहित द्वारा शान्ति आदि अनुपठानों के बाद शास्त्रज शिल्पविद्ध स्थपति कर्म करे 174
पुरोहित अग्नि में हवन करे, ज्योतिपी स्थरता दे, स्थपति भेट पूजा करे - इस प्रकार शान्ति की योजना करे 175
जब नगर के मर्म (केन्द्र) में, चौराहे पर स्थायी रूप से स्थापित देवता निरन्तर पूर्ण जाते हैं तब उस नगर में शान्ति रहती है 176
note: Roles at a city's founding: astrologer and priest perform śānti, the priest offers oblation, the astrologer fixes stability, the sthapati makes offerings.
gloss: Work done without shastra knowledge, without characteristics and without the rites is inauspicious and fruitless; after the astrologer and priest perform the propitiatory rites, the shastra-knowing sthapati should do the work; the priest offers oblation in fire, the astrologer gives stability, the sthapati makes offerings; when deities installed at the city's centre and crossroads are constantly worshipped, peace prevails in that city.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote:
सुवर्णकार सहित सभी अग्निजीवी और अन्य मजदूरों को आग्नेय (पूर्व-दक्षिण) दिशा में वसाये 189
वैश्य-व्यापारी, जुआड़ी-धूतं, चक्रिक (तेली, कुक्शर, मुखविर) तथा नट-नर्तकों के घर दक्षिण में बनवाये 190
note: Quarters of the city by occupation begin: fire-workers and goldsmiths south-east; merchants, gamblers, actors south.
gloss: Settle all those who live by fire, including goldsmiths, and other labourers in the south-east; build in the south the houses of vaishya merchants, gamblers and rogues, oil-pressers and actors and dancers.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote:
विप्र पूर्व दिशाभाग में, क्षत्रिय पश्चिम में, वैश्य और शूद्र क्रमशः दक्षिण तथा उत्तर में किये जायें 1100
वणिक, वैद्य और मुख्य लोगों को घारों दिशाओं में वसायें । विशेषतः सेना को घारों दिशाओं में स्थापित करें ।101
नगर से वाहर पूर्व दिशा में लिंगस्थों (शैव या विभिन्न सम्प्रदायों) को वसायें । भशान और उसके निवासियों को ज्ञानी स्थपति दक्षिण में वसायें ।102
note: Varṇas assigned to directions; Śaiva/sectarian ascetics (liṅgasthas) settled east outside the town, cremation ground south.
gloss: Brahmins in the east, kshatriyas in the west, vaishyas and shudras in the south and north respectively; merchants, physicians and chiefs in all four directions; the army especially on the four sides; outside the town in the east settle the lingasthas (Shaiva or sectarians); the wise sthapati should place the cremation ground and its inhabitants in the south.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote:
यूअरवाले, भेड़ पालक, शिकारी, मछुआरे, दमनाधिकृत (दण्ड वाले अधिकारी) आहे नैन्ध्त्य दिशा में वसाये जाये 191
जो रथ और आयुध में कुशल हों वे सव नगर की परिश्रम दिशा में वसाये जाये 192
विभिन्न कर्मों के अधिकारी, सेवक, सुराजीवी कलाल आदि वायव्य दिशा में वसाये 193
यतियों के आश्रय, ब्रह्मवत्स (ब्राह्मण/ब्रह्मचारी) की सभा, प्रपा (प्याऊ) और पुण्यशाला (सदावर्त, मनिर्दर, धर्मशालादि) उत्तर में दिशा में वनवायें 194
घी तथा फल के विक्रता ईशान (पूर्वांत्तर) दिशा में वंसाये जाये तो उचित है 195
note: Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra's allotment of city quarters by occupation: swineherds and hunters south-west, charioteers west, officials north-west, ascetics' shelters, Brahmin assembly and rest-houses north, ghee and fruit sellers north-east.
gloss: Swineherds, shepherds, hunters, fishermen and officers of punishment in the south-west; those skilled in chariots and weapons in the west; officials of various works, servants and liquor-sellers in the north-west; shelters of ascetics, the Brahmin assembly, water-sheds and charitable halls (punyashala) in the north; ghee and fruit sellers in the north-east.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: इन प्रस्थों में सर्वाधिक लोकप्रिय वल्लाल का भोजप्रवंध है । इसमें भोज, कालिदास और अन्य अनेक कवियों से सर्वन्धित छोटी-छोटी घटनाएँ हैं । वे सव मिलकर काव्यात्मक वातावरण वना देती हैं ।
note: Ballāla's Bhojaprabandha as the most popular of the many later works praising Bhoja - tradition rather than record.
gloss: Among these works the most popular is Ballala's Bhojaprabandha, with short anecdotes about Bhoja, Kalidasa and many other poets, which together create a poetic atmosphere.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: शुभशील के भोजप्रबंध में कतिपय कथाएँ वल्लाल की पुस्तक जैसी भी हैं। रल्ननंदन गणि (1340 ई.) भोजप्रबंध में कतिपय कथाएँ वल्लाल की पुस्तक जैसी भी हैं । पद्मपुस्त ने भी किसी या रल्नमंदिर गणि (1460 ई.) के भोजप्रबंध में सात खंड हैं । पद्मपुस्त ने भी किसी भोजप्रबंध की रचना की थी । राजशेखर (सूरि?) का भी भोजप्रबंध रचा बताया जाता है । वत्सराजकृत भोजप्रबंध (वारहवीं सदी) का भी उल्लेख मिलता है ।
note: List of later Bhojaprabandha works with dates (1340, 1460 CE; 12th-century Vatsarāja).
gloss: Shubhashila's Bhojaprabandha shares stories with Ballala's; Ratnanandana Gani (1340 CE) and Ratnamandira Gani (1460 CE) wrote Bhojaprabandhas (the latter in seven sections); Padmagupta, Rajashekhara (Suri?) and Vatsaraja (twelfth century) are also mentioned.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: इनके अतिरिक्त राजस्थानी, अवधी सहित विभिन्न भापाओं के काव्यग्रन्थों में भी भोज उपस्थित है। नरपति नाह् के बीसलदेव रासो, जायसी के पद्रायत, सिंढायय, दयालदास के पंवारवंशदर्पण, वाँकीदास री ख्यात, मालदेव के भोजचरित्र राहा और भोजचरित्र चौपाई, सारंग के भोजप्रवंध चतुप्पदी और भोजचरितरास, उदयभानु के भोजरासों, देवभद्र सूरि के श्रेयांसचरित, मुल्हण कवि के भोज राजा परकाया प्रदेशिनी पंद्रहवीं विशा कथा, हेमाणंद के भोज चरित्ररास, माघ का संवाद, कुशलधीर के भोजराजा चौपाई इत्यादि में इस राजा भोज के विषय में यथार्थ एवं कल्पित विभिन्न कथाएँ प्राप्त होती हैं।
note: Bhoja appears in Rajasthani, Avadhi etc. literature with both real and imagined stories - later tradition.
gloss: Bhoja is present in verse works in various languages including Rajasthani and Avadhi; Jayasi's Padmavat, Dayaldas's Panwar-vansh-darpan, Bankidas's khyat, Maldev's Bhojacharitra and others contain both real and imagined tales of Raja Bhoja.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

book_title: भोजदेव (Bhojadeva)
quote: इसीलिए कविजन अपने आय्यदाता की "नवभोज राज" अपथि से प्रशंसा करते थे। इस भोज के वंशज तेरहवीं सदी के अन्त में हुए अन्य राज भोज की प्रशंसा इस पूर्वज भोज की उपमा से की गयी - भोजो भोज इवापर:।
note: Poets praised patrons as 'Nava-Bhoja-rāja'; a later (late-13th-century) descendant was praised as 'Bhoja like another Bhoja' - memory of Bhoja as model.
gloss: Hence poets praised their patron with the epithet 'New Bhojaraja'; a descendant of this Bhoja, another king Bhoja at the end of the thirteenth century, was praised by comparison with this ancestor: 'Bhoja is Bhoja's equal'.
tier_note: T9 heritage or popular narrative: modern Hindi work, author and year unknown: attribute; corroborate before relying on it

quote: In the lower field of the left side and below the last line of the second plate is incised the representation of flying Garuda, the symbol of the Paramāra house of Mālava, holding a snake in his right arm and with the left hand raised above as if to

quote: 144; and it also appears to be in consonance with the well-known fact that Krishna III, or his successor Khottīga, according to a different view, led an expedition into Mālwā against the Paramāra ruler Siyaka, probably necessitated by the latter's assumption of the title of Maharājaadhirajapati (11. 12-13) in the present grants and thus proclaiming his independence.
note: Krishna III's expedition into Mālwā against the Paramāra Siyaka, possibly prompted by Siyaka's title Maharājādhirājapati proclaiming his independence.

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: Siyaka of both the present inscriptions is evidently identical with his namesake, the father of Vākpati-Muñja, as we know from the latter's Dharampuri, Ujjain and Gaōnri grants, issued respectively in V. 1031 (975 A.C.), 1036 (980 A.C.) and 1038 and 1043 (981 and 986 A.C.).¹ The first of these grants was issued 25 years later than the present records, which is just the period of one generation, as pointed out by the editors of these grants in the Ep Ind.; and that Śiyaka is also the same ruler for whom we have another date, viz. V. 1026, or 969 A.C. This shows that he held the throne at least from 949 to 969 A.C., which too is roughly a period of one generation.
note: Siyaka, father of Vākpati-Muñja, held the throne at least from 949 to 969 A.C., from grants of V. 1005, 1026 and Muñja's grants of 1031-1043.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: The inscription then proceeds to trace the genealogy of the Paramāra house of Mālwā. It tells us in vv. 5-6 that a hero who had sprung from the fire-altar of Vasishtha on the Mount Arbuda (Ābū) slew the enemies and brought back the cow of the sage which Viśvāmitra had taken away, and was, in reward of this deed, given the name of Paramāra (slayer of the foes) by Vasishtha who also blessed him with kingship. \( ^{2} \)  This account is purely legendary, a later creation, and can mean nothing more than to invent a high origin for the house, calling the Paramāras as belonging to agni-kula, exactly similar to that of the races born from the Sun and the moon. \( ^{3} \)  The present inscription, as we may note here, is the first to mention this legend, which is echoed in the later epigraphical records of the house, e.g., in the Nagpur Museum inscription and the Mändhātā copper-plate grant of Jayasimha II, as we shall see below.
note: Praśasti verses 5-6: hero sprung from Vasishtha's fire-altar on Mount Arbuda receives the name Paramāra; editor calls it 'purely legendary, a later creation', first mentioned in this inscription.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: Verses 8-11 mention the names of Vairisinha, Siyaka, Vākpati and another (a second) Vairisinha, each of whom was the son of his predecessor. The description here is purely conventional, except that we learn that the last of these rulers, viz., Vairisinha, was also known as Vajraṭa. Indirectly it also suggests that Vākpati fixed his capital at Dhārā. Here it is worth noting that of all these five rulers from Upēndrāraja to Vairisinha, the Nagpur prasasti gives only the last name, the Tilakamaṇāyari only that of Vairisinha, and the Navasāhasānika-charita which gives the name of Upēndrāraja, omits those of Vairisinha (I) and Siyaka (I). Thus the present inscription is the only record which gives a complete genealogy of the earlier Paramāra rulers of Mālwā, as already stated before.
note: Verses 8-11 name Vairisinha, Siyaka, Vākpati and a second Vairisinha (Vajraṭa); the only record giving a complete genealogy of the earlier Paramāra rulers.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: The next three verses (13-15) speak of Siyaka's son Vākpatirāja, who is stated to have been well-versed in the Sāstras and a poet too. The N.S. Charita calls him Utpalarāja (XI, 92). In the Nagpur prasasti we have the name Muñja instead of Vākpati; and Hall recognises first the identity of the two names. The land-grants call him Vākpati and add that he was also known as Amōghavarsha and bore the titles of Prithvī-vallabha and Śrī-vallabha. The praise given by the present prasasti to Vākpati is not undeserved, as we know from the various quotations of his verses in anthologies, works on alaṅkāvas, the Prabandhacintāmaṇi and the Bhōjaprabandha, etc., though some of these may be of a doubtful nature.
note: Verses 13-15 praise Vākpati (Muñja) as versed in the Śāstras and a poet; known by other names in other records.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

quote: In verse 8, which begins the genealogy, the inscription mentions the name Upēndrarāja, adding that he was born in the lineage of Paramāra and that “he acquired the high honour of kinghood by his prowess”. This indirectly goes to indicate that he was the first of the Paramāra kings of Mālwā. The land grants, on the other hand, mention the originator of the house to be Krishnarāja; and Dr. Hall and Cunningham have therefore taken both these names to be identical. Bühler also drew our attention to the fact that both these names are identical, and he further suggested that Upēndrarāja was probably the poetical form of the name and Krishnarāja was its Prakrit equivalent to be used in every day life.
note: Verse 8 names Upēndrarāja as first Paramāra king of Mālwā; land grants name Krishnarāja, taken by Hall, Cunningham and Bühler as the same.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

quote: From Mērutunga we learn that Vākpati invaded the Chālukya territories which touched the southern borders of his kingdom, as many as six times; but when in his seventh expedition in that land he crossed the Gōdāvarī, ignoring the advice of his minister Rudrāditya, he was taken prisoner by the Chālukya king Tailapa, who first treated him honourably, but an attempt to escape being detected, assassinated him. \( ^{2} \)  This story is corroborated by Chālukya inscriptions. \( ^{3} \)  This tragic event must have taken place between 993-94 and 997-998 A.C., the first of these dates being furnished by Amitagati who then composed his Subhāshutatvamsandōha, \( ^{4} \)  and the second is known to be the last year of Tailapa.
note: From Mērutuṅga: Vākpati taken prisoner and killed by Tailapa after crossing the Godāvarī; event placed between 993-94 and 997-98 A.C.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

quote: It must be admitted here, however, that we have no details regarding Sindhurāja's victories over all these powers: but he must have taken at least seven or eight years to perform all these military exploits before Padmagupta, who too alludes to some of them, must have completed his work. In view of this, Bühler has concluded that this prince must have reigned at least up to the middle of the first decade of the eleventh century when Padmagupta wrote. How much longer Sindhurāja may have ruled is not known: but he must have certainly closed some time before 1011 A.C.
note: Sindhurāja must have reigned into the first decade of the eleventh century, closing before 1011 A.C., earliest date of Bhōja.

quote: \( ^{1} \)  Verses 7-9 describe the scene of a battle which, from the description, appears to have been very fierce; and though the name of the Paramāra king who fought it is lost, he appears to have been no other than Siyaka II, from the fact that his son and successor Muñjadēva is described in the verses that immediately follow (10-12). Muñja is said to have been a valorous prince who defeated his enemies: these enemies are not mentioned by name, but they seem to have been the Chālukyas or the Chaulukyas with whom he is known to have waged wars. Verses 13-15 mention (Muñja's younger brother) Sindhurāja; and the next five verses (16-20) are devoted to the description of (his son) Bhōjadēva eulogising his learning and munificence in a conventional manner. After Bhōja is mentioned Jayasinha (lam-anu), who is stated to have been a great warrior vanquishing all his enemies; but the statement that he subjugated the earth bounded by the four oceans is again conventional and historically worthless.
note: Pānāhedā prasasti verses on Siyaka II, Muñja, Sindhurāja, Bhoja and Jayasiṃha; editor judges the Jayasiṃha world-conquest statement conventional and historically worthless.

quote:
The inscription refers itself to the reign of the illustrious Bhōjadēva who is called in it ‘the moon among the kings’ and who has been identified with the great literary person of that name and the king of Dhārā. The purpose of the inscription is to record the installation of the image of Vāgdevī, on the pedestal of which it is engraved. The year of the record, as mentioned in figures only and without any further details thereof, is 1091, which is equivalent to 1033-1034 A.C. The sculpture was engraved by Manathala, son of the mason Sahira, and the inscription was written by Sivadēva.
As we know from the Tilakamanjari, the palace of Bhōja or Bhōja-sālā as it is now popularly known, was then called Bhāratī-bhavana or Sarasvatīkaṇthābharaṇa, \( ^{3} \) and the image under reference may have been installed in it, in a prominent place, by Bhōja himself, who was a zealous devotee of the goddess Sarasvatī.
note: Sarasvatī image inscription of V.S. 1091 (1033-34 A.C.) refers to Bhōjadēva, identified with the learned king of Dhārā; Bhōja a zealous devotee of Sarasvatī, image possibly installed in the Bhōja-śālā.

quote:
To review the contents of the record, the first of the two extant plates begins with the description of a king of the name of Bhōjadēva who slew numbers of the soldiers of his enemies by his valour and enjoyed a long reign. This statement is only in general terms and has no historical value. The name of the family of this ruler along with those of his predecessors appears to have been mentioned in the first plate which is lost; but it is not difficult to know that he was no other than the homonymous Paramāra king who issued the Mahauḍi and the other charters edited here and whose kingdom included in it the Sābarkāṃthā-Ahmedabad region, as we know from his grandfather Sīyaka's grants of the Harsōlā plates and from one of his feudatories at Mōḍāsā, which have been dealt with above.\( ^{2} \)
The inscription on then introduces the name of Bhōja's feudatory\( ^{3} \) Sūrāditya, who had migrated from Kānyakubja (Kanauj) and who had been born in the family of the Śravaṇabhadras. This hero is further stated to have killed his overlord's enemy warriors and thus rendered the sovereignty of the latter firm.
note: Tilakwādā plates: Bhōja's feudatory Sūrāditya helped him against enemies; kingdom included the Sābarkāṃthā-Ahmedabad region.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

quote: Verse 20 of the prāsasti states that Bhōja ‘covered the world all around with temples dedicated to Kēdāra, Rāmēśvara, Sōmanātha, Sunḍīra (?), Kāla, Anala and Rudra.’ The first three of these names appear to be intended to refer, respectively, to the well-known Śiva temples in the north, south and west; and following the same, the fourth, which is a strange and so-far-unknown name, may possibly have been one in the east. quote:
The inscription belongs to the reign of the Panambhattāraka, Mahārājādhurāja, Paramēśvara, the illustrious Jayasimhadēva, who was evidently a member of the Paramāra house of Dhāra. The object of it is to record the grant, by Jayasimhadēva, of the village Bhima, situated in the territorial division of Maktulā-forty-two in the Pūrnapathaka-mangala, for the maintenance of the Brāhmaṇas residing in the patta-sālā (tent-house) at the holy Amarēśvara, for the religious merit of his parents and himself. The date is given in 1. 29 in decimal figures only: it is the thirteenth of the dark half of Āshāḍha of the (Vikrama) Sanivat 1112. For the expired Chatrīādī year 1112, this date would correspond to 27th May, 1055 A.C., and for the expired Kārtthāḍī year to 13th June or 13th July, 1056 A.C.\(^{1}\) It does not admit of verification.
After two maṇḍula-sākās which are generally to be found in the several grants of the Paramāra king and which pay homage to Īyōma-kāśa and Śmar-ārātī (both meaning Siva), the inscription gives the genealogy of the king Jayasimha, beginning with the P.M.R., the illustrious Vākpatirājadeva, his successor the P.M.P., the illustrious Sindhurājadeva, his successor the P.M.P., the illustrious Bhājadeva, and his successor the P.M.P., the illustrious Jayasimhadeva (ll. 3-6).
note: Mandhata grant of Jayasimhadēva (V.S. 1112, 27 May 1055 A.C. or 1056): Paramāra genealogy Vākpati, Sindhurāja, Bhōja, Jayasimha; grant for Brāhmaṇas at Amarēśvara.

quote: The name of Jayasiniha is not known from any other inscription of the house—not even from the Udaipur and Nagpur prasats which give an almost complete list of kings ruling at Dhara up to the time when they were engraved. On the other hand, Bhojadêva is generally taken to have been succeeded by Udayadilva who is now definitely known to be his brother. But the present record, which mentions Jayasimha as the immediate successor of Bhojadêva and the evidence of which cannot be doubted for any reason, definitely shows that Jayasiniha must be placed between Bhojadêva and Udayadilva and thus between 1047 and 1080 A.C. which are respectively the latest and the earliest known years of these two rulers.
note: Jayasimha is absent from the Udaipur and Nagpur praśastis; Bhōja generally taken as succeeded by Udayāditya, now known to be his brother, but this record places Jayasimha between 1047 and 1080 A.C.

quote: The inscription thus reveals for the first time a new historical fact, viz. that Lakshmadēva predeceased both Udayāditya and Naravarman, though the circumstances leading to his death, along with the approximate time when it took place, are not known. Here we have also to note that the Nagpur Museum stone inscription, which enumerates the names of all the rulers from Vairisinha to Lakshmadēva, while introducing each one of them, uses such a word as signifies 'a king', e.g., kshutipati, bhūpati or ūripa, but such a word is not used in it in the case of the last of them only, i.e. Lakshmadēva, though it states that he was devoted to govern the subjects. \( ^{4} \)  The omission of a word denoting a king only with the name of Lakshmadēva in the record is significant as it perhaps implies to show that he never ascended the throne of Dhāra. That he worked as governor in some of the eastern part of the Paramāra dominions under his father Udayāditya is also suggested by the donation made by him as recorded in the same inscription.
note: New fact that Lakshmadēva predeceased both Udayāditya and Naravarman; omission of a royal title suggests he never ascended the throne of Dhāra; he perhaps governed in the eastern Paramāra dominions.

quote: The inscription refers itself to Udayāditya who is endowed in it with the titles of Paramabhattāraka, Mahāvājādhiraja and Paramēśvara, and is stated to have then encamped at the village Dhavalī near Ujjain. \( ^{1} \)  The purpose of the inscription is to record the donation made by Naravarman, who was evidently his son, of 12 halas (?) of land in the village known as Rādhaghatikā, for perpetually burning a lamp (akshaya-dīpikā) in honour of Lakshmadēva who was another son of Udayāditya and thus a brother of Naravarman. The year, mentioned in numerical figures in the last line of the inscription, is 1140, without any further details. As the current Vikrama year, it corresponds to 1082 A.C. The name of the engraver is not recorded, nor is any epithet attached either to the name of Naravarman or to that of Lakshmadēva.

quote: Lakshmadēva and Naravarman are the well-known sons of Udayāditya: but the expression denoting the purpose of the donation made here calls our special attention. It is akshaya-dīpi-kāthē, which appears to have been used for its longer and complete form, viz., akshaya-lōka-dīpi-kāthē, in the sense of “a lamp giving perpetual happiness in heaven”. And taken in this sense, which appears to be the only possibility, the inscription contains a very important historical reference, leading us to conclude that Lakshmadēva had died a short time before the record was executed. Naravarman had a great affection for his brother Lakshmadēva, as we know from the Nagpur Museum stone inscription which was composed by the former ruler who devoted as many as 19 stanzas giving fulsome praise to the description of Lakshmadēva.
note: Lakshmadēva and Naravarman are well-known sons of Udayāditya; the expression 'akshaya-dīpikā' implies Lakshmadēva had died shortly before.

quote: The following verse (21) introduces Udayāditya, who is spoken of as 'another Sun dispelling the dense darkness in the form of his magnanimous foes with the rays issuing from his strong sword and thereby gladdening the hearts of his people by his splendour'. The enemies referred to here are not specified, but the description goes to indicate that they were very powerful and had deprived the Paramāras of their kingdom in the last days of Bhōja, or immediately after his death. From the Prabandhachintāmaṇi we learn that in the last days of Bhōjadēva the Kalachuri Karṇa and the Chaulukya Bhīma attacked Mālwā simultaneously and took possession of his kingdom. This statement is corroborated by epigraphical records of the Paramāras. The Nagpur prasasti, which is more explicit on the point, states that Udayāditya resembled the Great Boar in delivering the earth (i.e., the Paramāra kingdom) which had submerged in the mighty oceans in the form of the Karṇāta, Karṇa and others (prabhriti). This description agrees very closely with that of the Mándhātā grant of Jayasinīha II, though the enemy mentioned there was only the Gurjara king.
note: Verse 21 introduces Udayāditya as 'another Sun'; after Kalachuri Karṇa and Chaulukya Bhīma took Bhōja's kingdom, the Nagpur praśasti says Udayāditya delivered the earth like the Great Boar.

quote: The importance of the present inscription, however, lies in the fact that the gift was made on the occasion of the annual funeral ceremony of Udayādiya in V.S. i152 or 1095 A.C., by his son Naravarman, whose earliest known date is supplied by the preceding inscription, \( ^{4} \) giving the year to be V.S. 1151 or 1094 A.C., which is ten years earlier than the earliest known date of the king, and here we have also to bear in mind that it is a private record. quote: Ind., Banerji observes that “the very fact that an ordinary feudatory chief dares to make a grant of land without referring the matter to his sovereign shows that the power of the Paramāras of Māiwā had weakened considerably at the time of the issue of the grant”.¹ But are we to follow the same line of thought and conclude that the Paramāra power was on its wane in about 1011 A.C. and also in 1046 A.C. when the Mōdāsā and the Tilakwādā grants were respectively issued by the others of his feudatories? Both these inscriptions too do not contain a word about the imperial king. On the other hand, if Bhōja's conquest of Kōknāṇa is to be placed some time between 1018 and 1020 A.C., the former being the year of his Mahaudī grant which does not mention this achievement and the latter of those found at Bētmā and Bānswādā which are explicit on the point, it is obvious that his power was then rather increasing; and knowing from history that he had to suffer only towards the end of his rule in the combined attack on his kingdom by the Chaulukyas and the Kalachuris and some time before, at the hands of the Chālukyas, it is difficult to agree with Banerji in his conclusion. Thus the present grant appears to have been issued much earlier than the disaster of the Paramāra kingdom which has already been discussed above.
note: Discussion whether Paramāra power was waning in 1011 and 1046; argues Bhōja's power was rather increasing until the late reverse.

quote: Verses 14-15 of the present record state that “his lotus-feet were coloured by the jewels on the heads of the Karnnāṭas, Lāṭas, Kéralas and Chōlas and he vanquished Yuvarāja, and slaying his general, as a victor, raised on high his sword in Tripuri.” The Kalachuri Yuvarāja of Tripuri (c. 980-990) who was Vākpati’s contemporary was a weak ruler, quite unlike his father Lakshmaṇa; and Vākpati may have come into a clash with Yuvarāja whose kingdom lay immediately to the east of Mālwā and scored a victory over him, though of a fleeting nature. It has to be admitted here, however, that we have no evidence in support of this assertion, nor is it possible to fix the date of this clash. With reference to Vākpati’s victory over the Karnātaṣ (evidently the Chālukyas), we know that in his long struggle with his adversary Trailapa II, he had to lose his throne and life in the end; and the claim of the prasasti that Vākpati subdued the Karnāṭas is evidently inadmissible. It is however possible that he may have gained some success in one of his earlier expeditions against the region and that success may have been referred to here.
note: Praśasti claims Vākpati's victories over Karnāṭas, Lāṭas, Keralas, Cholas and the Kalachuri Yuvarāja; editor finds the Karnāṭa claim 'evidently inadmissible' and lacks evidence for the Yuvarāja clash.

quote:
Bühler contends that the story of Bhōja's reverse narrated by the Prabandhachintāmaṇi and also by the epigraphical records of the house cannot be implicitly accepted because it does not find place in the inscriptions of the Kalachuris; nor does Hémachandra, who extols Bhima 'in the best possible light' and who wrote his Dvyāśraya-kāvya about 150 years before Mērutunga, say anything about it. But here we are to remember that it was a long-drawn war and the story does not end with the reverse sustained by Bhōja but with the 'total destruction (saṅhāra) of the Kalachuri king (Dāhal-ādhiśa) at the hands of Udayāditya,' as we know from 1.2 of the following inscription, which is in continuation of the inscription in hand and was discovered 37 years after Bühler worked out his article.
The next verse (22), which is the last complete verse of the prasasti, again glorifies Udayā-ditya, stating that 'for him who restored the earth (from the enemies) it was easy to restore the Premial Boar.' This statement appears to be a hint to the restoration of a Boar-temple by Udayāditya, as we shall see in the inscription that follows (Part B).
note: Bühler doubts the story of Bhōja's reverse; editor cites the 'total destruction' of the Kalachuri king by Udayāditya, and verse 22 hints at restoration of a Boar-temple by Udayāditya.

quote: As we shall presently see, the localities showing the situation of the gift land were all lying in the western Betwā valley, just opposite to that region which included in it places like Jhansi, Lalitpur and Dēogaḍh on the east of the river which was a part of the Chandēlla kingdom, since 1193 A.C., as we know that Kīrtivarman's general Vatsarāja had built a ghatta on this river and he had also established himself in this region. quote: The whole discussion on the division of the Paramāra kingdom during the fourth decade of the twelfth century may be summarised here. Soon after the capture of Mālava and its king Yasōvarman, by the Chaulukya Jayasinha, in 1138 A.C., the former's sons Jayavarman and Lakshmīvarman (and along with them Trailōkyavarman also, about whom we shall speak while editing his inscription), left the capital Dhāra and had their resort in the easternmost part of Mālwa—somewhere in the region around Bhopāl, where they annexed some territories from the Chandellas and established themselves there.
note: Summary: after Chaulukya Jayasinha captured Yaśōvarman in 1138 A.C., his sons left Dhāra for the Bhopāl region and annexed territory from the Chandellas.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: Jayavarman has been omitted in the present record, and also that Lakshmīvarman's name has similarly been omitted in the Pipliñāgar grant of Haris-chandra, of Sañvat 1235 (1178 A.C.),¹ Kielhorn observes as follows, with reference to the succession in the family of Yaśōvarman: "Yaśōvarman had three sons, Jayavarman, Ajayavarman and Lakshmīvarman; and he was in the first instance succeeded by Jayavarman. Soon after his succession (and certainly some time between Vikrama 1192 and 1200), Jayavarman was dethroned by Ajayavarman, who and whose successors then became the main branch of the Paramāra family in Mālwā, and continued to style themselves Mahāvājas. The third brother Lakshmīvarman, however, did not submit to Ajayavarman, and as stated in E (i.e. the Bhopāl grant of the Mahākumāra Udayavarman), he succeeded by force of arms in appropriating a portion of Mālwā, which he and his son and grandson de facto ruled over as independent chiefs. At the same time, Lakshmīvarman, and, after him, his son and successor Hariśchandra looked upon Jayavarman, though deposed, as the rightful sovereign of Mālava, and, in my opinion, it is for this reason that Hariśchandra, in the grant D (his Pipliñanagar grant) professes to rule by the favour of that prince, and that both Lakshmīvarman and Hariśchandra claim for themselves no higher title than that of Mahākumāra, a title which was handed down to, and adopted by, even Lakshmīvarman's grandson Udayavarman."²
note: Kielhorn's view of the succession in Yaśōvarman's family (Jayavarman, Ajayavarman, Lakshmīvarman); a scholarly debate on the Paramāra division.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: Moreover, the statement of the Bhopāl grant of Udayavarman to the effect that Lakshmīvarman succeeded in occupying the territory not from Jayavarman, who, as we have seen in the preceding grant, had himself fled to the Bhopāl region and may have then been accompanied by Lakshmīvarman, but from his enemies who were the Chandēlas who had by that time usurped a portion of the region around Bhilsā, as we know from the Augasī grant of Madanavarman,\(^{3}\) which was issued from his residence near Bhillasānipura: and our observation gets further support from the fact that Lakshmīvarman confirmed the grant made by his father in the same region around Bhilsā which is herein called the Mahādvādaśaka-mandala: and it may fairly be imagined that Lakshmīvarman's reconquest of the region may probably have necessitated the re-issuing of the grant.
note: Chandēlas had usurped a portion of the region around Bhilsā, per the Augasī grant of Madanavarman.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: and resumed the government, proclaiming himself as a sovereign lord: and the younger brother Lakshmīvarman continued to remain in the Bhopāl region as a subordinate ruler, where he and his descendants governed the territory and were satisfied with the lower title of Mahā-kumāru. Professor Hall's theory that Lakshmīvarman was the elder of the two,\(^{1}\) cannot be accepted as it is not based on any substantial evidence: and the very fact that Jayavarman is called a Mahārajādhiñāja not only in his but also in the grants issued by the Mahākumāras who were the descendants of Lakshmīvarman, goes against Hall's observations.
note: Jayavarman resumed government at Dhāra as sovereign; Lakshmīvarman stayed in Bhopāl region with the lower title Mahākumāra.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: As for the localities mentioned in the inscription, Dhārā (l. 6) is obviously the modern Dhār, now the principal town of a district of the same name; and the maṇḍala mentioned by the name of Mahādvādaśaka (l. 5) comprised parts of the modern districts of Bhilsā (now called Vidishā) and Bhopāl: this maṇḍala is also mentioned in the Bhopāl charter of Lakshmīvarman's son Harischandra, below, No.
note: The Mahādvādaśaka maṇḍala comprised parts of modern Bhilsā (Vidishā) and Bhopāl districts.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: Hariśchandra, the son of Lakshmīvarman, is known to have issued a grant from the same place vidishā, only a couple of years earlier in the (Vikrama) year 1214: and in view of all these findings the only conclusion that can be drawn is that Trailōkyavarman of the present inscription undoubtedly belonged to that branch of the Paramāras who called themselves Mahā-kumāras in their inscriptions and the earliest of whom is known to be Lakshmīvarman. \( ^{2} \)  This again goes to support the view that Trailōkyavarman appears to have acted as a regent during the minority of his nephew Harischandra, and as such, he also enjoyed the titles connected with the princes of the Mahākumāra line and had full powers of a chief. \( ^{3} \)  This finds strange corroboration in the fact that in his Bhopāl grant Harischandra states that he obtained his rulership through the favour of the Mahākumāra Trailōkyavarman.
note: Trailōkyavarman belonged to the Mahākumāra branch of Paramāras, apparently regent during nephew Harischandra's minority; Harischandra had issued a grant from Vidishā in V.S. 1214.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: The grant was made, as seen above, on the ninth day of a month, the name of which is lost along with the figures showing the year, at the end of 1.2, by the Mahākumāra Trailōkyavarma-dēva, who is mentioned as samasta-prakriyā-virājamāna and also bearing all the royal titles. The pedigree of this prince and the name of the house to which he belonged are not specified in the record; but from the title of Mahākumāra attached to his name in it, he is evidently to be considered a member of the subordinate branch of the Paramāra house ruling over the region around Bhopāl and may be identified with the homonymous prince mentioned in the Bhopāl charter of the Paramāra Mahākumāra Harischandradeva, who is stated to have achieved his victory and kingship through this prince (-prasād-āvāpta-vujay-ādhupatyah).
note: Gyāraspur grant by Mahākumāra Trailōkyavarmadēva, evidently of the subordinate Paramāra branch around Bhopāl; pedigree not specified.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: In view of this consideration, it does not appear to be impossible that Harischandra was very young when he succeeded his father Lakshmivarman, as also pointed out by Chakravarti. Moreover, we may also hold with the same scholar that during Harischandra’s minority, his uncle, Trailōkyavarman, acted as a regent, and as such, he also enjoyed the titles connected with the princes of this line and wielded the full power of a chief who could also issue a grant.
note: Following Chakravarti, Trailōkyavarman acted as regent during Harischandra's minority.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: The charter then refers to the predecessors of the donor, giving the names of the Paramabhattāraka, Mahārājādhirāja and Paramēśvara, the glorious Naravarmadēva and his successor the P.M.P. the illustrious Yasōvarmadēva (ll. 3-4). After Yasōvarmadēva we have the names of Trailōkyavarmadēva and then of the doner Haríschandradēva, each of whom is mentioned as endowed with all praise and enjoying the right to the five great musical sounds. The record also supplies the additional information that the later of these two rulers obtained his principality through the favour of the former (-pāda-prasād-avāpla-vijay-adhapatyah).
note: Harischandra's grant names Naravarmadēva, Yasōvarmadēva, Trailōkyavarmadēva and Harischandra; Harischandra obtained his principality through Trailōkyavarman's favour.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: Comparing the evidence supplied by the present and the following grants of Harischandra, we notice another inconsistency, viz., that whereas the former of these charters states that Harischandra obtained his territory through the favour of the Mahākumāra Trailōkyavarman, the latter gives this credit not to Trailōkyavarman but to the P.M.P. Jayavarman. But here we have to note the actual wordings of the two grants; for whereas the former uses the expression vujay-ādhuṣatya, meaning that Harischandra obtained some victory (over an enemy), the latter has the expression nij-ādhuṣatya, indicating that he received the principality from (through the sanction of) Jayavarman who was then the Imperial sovereign. To obtain sanction of the Imperial house, which was ruling at Dhārā, by the subordinate ruler in the Bhopāl region may have been a matter of necessity; and the Pipliānagar grant points to the same. The victory referred to in the present charter may possibly allude to one against the Chandēlas who were their northern neighbours.
note: Two Harischandra grants credit different sovereigns (Trailōkyavarman, Jayavarman); victory may allude to the Chandēlas, their northern neighbours.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: Like many other Paramāra grants, the present record opens with two verses in honour of the god Śiva, and they are followed by prose passages containing the genealogy of the donor, mentioning the names of the Paramabhattāraka, Mahārājādhirāja and Paramēśvara Udayāditya, his successor the P.M.P. Naravarman, his successor the P.M.P. Yaśōvarman, and the latter's successor Jayavarman. This genealogy is the same as known from the other records of the house. But the information that follows is new; it states that Hariśchandra, who enjoyed the five great sounds and was a Mahākumāra, obtained his principality through the last-mentioned ruler, i.e., Jayavarman (ētasmāt-prishtatama-prabhōh prasād-āvāpta-nijādhipathy).
note: Piplianagar grant genealogy: Udayāditya, Naravarman, Yaśōvarman, Jayavarman; Hariśchandra obtained his principality through Jayavarman.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: The importance of the present record, however, lies in the fact that it tells us that Hariśchandra was the son of Lakshmīvarman, as mentioned in the sign-manual of the king in the end. In fact this is the only record to mention this relationship. Another importance of the present inscription lies in the fact that Hariśchandra succeeded in extending the boundaries of his kingdom to the south of the Narmadā, as we shall see below while identifying the localities mentioned therein. For whereas all the other grants made by the rulers of the Mahākumāra branch of the Paramāra house refer to the region lying to the north of the river, the present one is the only grant made by a prince belonging to that house in the Hoshangābād District, which extends to the south of the Narmadā.
note: Hariśchandra was son of Lakshmīvarman; he extended his kingdom south of the Narmadā into Hoshangābād District.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: The genealogical portion (ll. 3 ff.) mentions the names of Yasōvarman and his successor Jayavarman, both as sovereign lords: and thereafter figures the name of Lakshmivarman, who is stated to have the privilege of using the five great sounds and was a Mahākumāra. He was succeeded by Harischandra, and Harischandra by his son Udayavarman,\(^{2}\) who issued the present grant. Both these rulers are mentioned as Mahākumāras, entitled to the use of the five great sounds, as Lakshmīvarman. Of the names figuring in the genealogy, those of Yasōvarman and his son Jayavarman, who were sovereign lords at Dhārā, are well known, and we also know that Lakshmīvarman was the latter's brother and had established himself in the Bhopāl
note: Udayavarman's grant (V.S. 1256) lists Yasōvarman, Jayavarman, Lakshmīvarman, Harischandra and Udayavarman; Lakshmīvarman established himself in the Bhopāl region as subordinate to the Imperial Paramāra house.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: Referring to that history, we know that Jayavarman's son Vindhyavarman succeeded in recovering his ancestral dominions from the Chaulukya Mūlarāja II, but he could not do so before the present grant was issued; for had he succeeded finally establishing himself in Mālvā, we would have, as rightly suggested by Dr. N. P. Chakravarti, found his name mentioned in the present grant. \( ^{1} \)  He had also to fight hard against his southern neighbours who were at that time rising, viz., Bhillama V of the Yādava house of Dēvagiri and Ballāla II Dōrāsamudra, \( ^{5} \)  before he could completely assert his authority over Mālvā.
note: Jayavarman's son Vindhyavarman recovered ancestral dominions from Chaulukya Mūlarāja II, after the present grant, and had to fight the Yādavas and Hoysalas.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: Verse 11 of the present record tells us that Yaśōvarman had a son named Ajayavarman (tasnād = Ajayaavarm = ābhāt); this expression is reproduced in the following two inscriptions of the king and in the Māndhāta grant of Devapāla and Jayavarman \( ^{2} \) ; whereas in the other set of records which are all in prose, \( ^{3} \)  the name of Yaśōvarman's son appears as Jayavarman; and this led Kielhorn to hold that Yaśōvarman had two sons with the names of Jayavarman and Ajayavarman who were two different persons. \( ^{4} \)  But when we consider that there is not even a single inscription which mentions both these names and also that there are two different sets of records—all those which are in prose invariably give the name to be Jayavarman and all those which are in poetry give it as Ajayavarman, the identity of both these persons is established beyond doubt, and it also follows that in the latter of these sets the name Jayavarman is changed to Ajayavarman only to suit the metre.
note: Poetic records name Yaśōvarman's son Ajayavarman, prose records Jayavarman; editor holds them identical, name changed to suit the metre (against Kielhorn).
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: The expression Gurjarōchchhēda-nurbandhī applied to Vindhyavarman in verse 12 has a reference to his success in liberating the Paramāra kingdom which had suffered a disastrous plight at the hands of the Chaulukyas since the days of Yaśovarman whose kingdom had been captured by Jayasinha Siddharāja, as seen above.
note: Vindhyavarman liberated the Paramāra kingdom suffered at Chaulukya hands since Yaśovarman, whose kingdom Jayasinha Siddharāja had captured.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: This is so far the earliest known inscription connecting Dēvapāla, a scion of the Mahākumāra line with the main branch of the Paramāra family ruling at Dhāra. \( ^{4} \)  The latest known year of Arjunavarman of the main branch is 1215 A.C. when he issued the Sehōre grant: and when and how his rule ended is not known; but the statement of the present inscription shows that he was succeeded by Dēvapāla, some time before 1218 A.C. The difficulty that presents itself in the present inscription, however, is the mention of both the contradictory titles, viz., that of a feudatory and of an independent chief, associated with the name of Dēvapāla. This was already noted by Kielhorn while editing it, but he did not arrive at a satisfactory solution of the problem. And in view of both the contradictory titles attached to Dēvapāla's name in the present record, it appears very probable that in the first instance, in the natural course, he succeeded his father Harišchandra with the title of Mahākumāra, \( ^{6} \)  and for some time he may have ruled as a subordinate prince of the main branch; but soon after, with the end of the rule of Arjunavarman who may have left behind him no worthy person in the main branch, the throne of Dhāriā was also held by Devapāla, who styled himself as Paramabhattāraka, Mahāraṣiādhnaṇa and Paramēśvara.
note: Earliest known record linking Dēvapāla of the Mahākumāra line to the main Paramāra house at Dhāra; he apparently succeeded Arjunavarman before 1218 A.C.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: The inscription does not specify Dêvapâla's relationship with Arjunavarman whom he is said to have succeeded, or the state of affairs leading to the former's accession. In this respect we have already seen in the preceding record that Arjunavarman of the main branch probably died without leaving a male heir, and Dêvapâla of the subordinate branch, who first succeeded his father Hariśchandra on the subordinate throne, seems to have had an opportunity of uniting both the houses and occupying the throne of Dhârâ.
note: Dēvapāla's relationship with Arjunavarman is not stated; Arjunavarman probably died without male heir and Dēvapāla may have united both houses at Dhārā.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: Bilhaṇa is evidently the same as the Mahā-sāndhi-vigrahika of Arjunaivarman's grandfather Vindhyavarman, as we know from Āśādhara's Dharmāmyrta. \( ^{1} \)  Āśādhara is known to have migrated to Mälwā from the Sapādaluksha country, which was conquered by Mahmūd Ghorī in 1192 A.C.; and Vindhyavarman must be taken on the throne of Dhārā almost during the same time in view of his contest with the Yādava Bhillama who ascended the throne of Dēvagiri in c. 1187 A.C. and was for a few initial years of his reign fully occupied in the south.
note: Bilhaṇa was minister of Vindhyavarman; dated via Āśādhara's migration after Mahmūd Ghorī's conquest of 1192 A.C. and Vindhyavarman's contest with Yādava Bhillama (c. 1187).
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: The inscription refers itself to the auspicious and victorious reign of the illustrious Dēvapālādeva, who is evidently identical with the homonymous Paramāra ruler of Dhārā, whose earliest known date is furnished by the Harsūd or Harsaudā inscription to be V. 1275 and another by the Māndhātā grant dated in V. 1282.
note: Dēvapāla is identical with the Paramāra ruler of Dhārā, whose earliest known date is Harsūd VS 1275 and another is the Māndhātā grant of VS 1282.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: This person was a son of Dēvapāla and the younger brother of Jaitugidēva, as we already know. And in view of the fact that Jaitugi's only date is recorded to be V. 1300 or 1243 A.C. \( ^{1} \) , the present inscription, which is the earliest of Jayasimha's reign, clearly indicates that he succeeded his elder brother Jaitugidēva sometime between 1243 and 1256 A.C. We also know that in Jaitugi's time Mālwā had suffered from the invasions of the Yādava Krishna from the south, of the Vāghēlas from the west, and also from the Muslim general Balban from the north: \( ^{5} \)  and the present inscription goes to indicate that in spite of all these odds, Jayavarman, besides maintaining the integrity of his kingdom, had successfully penetrated so far in the Saugor (Sāgar) District, following the foot-steps of his father, whose records are found in the Khanḍwā District which is to its west.
note: Jayasimha (Jayavarman), younger brother of Jaitugidēva, succeeded him between 1243 and 1256 A.C.; Mālwā had suffered Yādava, Vāghēla and Balban invasions under Jaitugi.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: 54) mentions a ruler, whose name is again lost but who is said to have put to flight (made kāndūśika) a Yadu king. This is evidently a reference to Arjunavarman's successor Devapāla who, by a stratagem to avoid invasion of his own country, concluded a treaty with the Yādava Sīṅhaṇa (1210-1247 A.C.) and entered with him into a confederacy to invade Gujarāt which was then passing through a crisis during the weak rule of Bhīma II.
note: Mōḍi inscription (Jayavarman II time): a ruler who put a Yadu king to flight read as Devapāla, who made a treaty with the Yādava Sīṅhaṇa (1210-1247).
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: The fragmentary nature of the inscription does not enable us to know if any other donation was recorded in it; but it reveals for the first time the name of Chāduri who was the Chief Minister of Javavarman, along with that of Arisimha, who is stated here to have been the grandson of Rājaputra Gōvinda and who is otherwise unknown.
note: Inscription reveals Chāduri as Chief Minister of Jayavarman; Arisimha grandson of Rājaputra Gōvinda otherwise unknown.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote:
The plates were issued by the Mahārdjādhivāja, the illustrious Jayavarmadeva, the younger brother of Jaitugideva. They record the perpetual grant of the village Vadaūda, situated in the Mahuada-pathaka, to three Brāhmanas, hailing from different localities. The (produce of the) village was divided into six shares (vaittakus), so that one of the donees obtained four shares, and the other two, one share each.
In its initial portion the charter cites the same verses (1-22) as found in Devapala's Mändhātā grant, containing the genealogy of the house from Bhōja to Dēvapāla; \( ^{1} \) and new information is added thereafter in two stanzas (vv. 22-23), the first of which states that Dēvapāla was succeeded on the throne of Mālava by his son Jaitugi, who bore the epithet of Bālānārāyaṇa: \( ^{2} \) The second of these stanzas means to say that Jaitugi was succeeded by his younger brother Jayavarman, This account is followed by recording the purpose.
note: Plates of Jayavarmadeva, younger brother of Jaitugideva; cite the genealogy from Bhōja to Dēvapāla; Dēvapāla succeeded by Jaitugi, then Jayavarman.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
tier_note: T1 contemporary inscription: inscriptions as edited in CII VII.2; for dynastic facts the editor's readings outrank Ganguly

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: And as none of the remaining six of the names mentioned here is so far known as belonging to the Paramāra house of Dhāra in an earlier period, they may be taken to be unhistorical and their description to be merely a creation of the poet's mind.
note: Editor takes six of the early names as unhistorical, a creation of the poet's mind: evidence versus tradition.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras
quote: This account too is equally confusive. The composer of the record, besides his ignorance of the fact that Vākpati and Muñja were the two names borne by the same king, ascribes Muñja's erudition to his predecessor Vākpati. Moreover, from his description it is not clearly known whether in the house there were one or two kings bearing the names of Vākpati and Sīyaka.

quote: That Vakpati and Muñja were names of one and the same king admits of no doubt. King Arjunavarman, in his commentary on Amarusātaka, known as Rasikasamjīvinī, states that Vakpatirāja, otherwise known as Muñja, was one of his predecessors. Similarly, there is ample evidence to prove his identity with the king Utpala. In the Navasāhasānka-carita, in one place Vakpati is spoken of as the elder brother of Sindhurāja, who followed him (on the throne) after his death. But in another place, where the history of the early Paramāra kings of Malwa is narrated, Sindhurāja is reported to have mounted the throne of Utpalarāja. Here the absolute omission of the name, Vakpatirāja, by the poet proves the identity of the two. This is further confirmed by the fact that the authorship of a verse ascribed to Utpalarāja by the Kashmirian poet Kṣemendra is attributed to Vakpatirāja by Vallabhadeva.
